short_description: An obligate intracellular bacterium with NO free-living form at all: it exists only as a tiny, tough, infectious elementary body (EB, ~0.2-0.3 µm) or as a larger, fragile, dividing reticulate body (RB, ~0.5-1 µm) growing inside a host-cell inclusion. The two-form cycle IS the subject -- no other microbe in this atlas has this shape. Infects the conjunctiva of cats above all, causing weeping, gummed-up eyes; NOT the same species as C. trachomatis (human STI/trachoma agent) even though it shares the same genus-level biology.
genus_vs_species_note: The developmental cycle (EB <-> RB, the inclusion, binary fission, no peptidoglycan, no flagella) is GENUS-LEVEL biology shared by every Chlamydia/Chlamydophila species (trachomatis, psittaci, pneumoniae, felis, etc.) and is what almost all citable primary literature and imagery documents, because C. trachomatis is the overwhelmingly best-studied species. The SPECIES-SPECIFIC facts for C. felis are: its near-exclusive conjunctival/upper-respiratory tropism in cats (vs. trachomatis' genital/ocular-trachoma tropism in humans), transmission via direct contact / ocular-nasal secretions in group-housed cats (shelters, catteries), the disease it causes (feline conjunctivitis / 'cat flu' component, not an STI), doxycycline as first-line treatment, an available (partially protective) vaccine, and rare/mild zoonotic transmission to immunocompromised people in close contact with an infected cat. This research keeps those two levels distinct throughout and the reference image (a real micrograph) is explicitly flagged as C. trachomatis, not C. felis, because no freely-licensed C. felis-specific micrograph could be found.

morphology_notes: GENUS-LEVEL (applies to all Chlamydia spp. including felis): a biphasic developmental cycle alternating between two structurally distinct forms. The elementary body (EB) is small (~0.2-0.3 µm, NCBI Bookshelf gives 0.25-0.3 µm; PLOS ONE ~0.3 µm), round, electron-dense under TEM, metabolically near-dormant, and has a rigid, cross-linked, cysteine-rich outer envelope that lets it survive outside a cell -- this is the infectious, transmitting form.

GENUS-LEVEL: the reticulate body (RB) is larger (~0.5-1 µm, NCBI Bookshelf gives 0.5-0.6 µm; other sources up to 1-1.5 µm as an RB grows before dividing), round, electron-lucent/pale under TEM (fewer dense granules, more open internal texture), metabolically active, and fragile -- it cannot survive outside a cell and cannot infect a new one; it only divides.
GENUS-LEVEL: neither form has flagella -- chlamydiae are nonmotile coccoid organisms at every life stage (NCBI Bookshelf). Do not draw any whip-like or hair-like appendage on either form.

GENUS-LEVEL, the 'chlamydial anomaly': chlamydiae are Gram-negative-like (inner + outer membrane, LPS) but their cell envelope conspicuously LACKS a substantial peptidoglycan layer -- rigidity in the EB instead comes from a cysteine-rich, disulfide-cross-linked outer-membrane protein complex (MOMP/OmcA/OmcB), not a peptidoglycan sacculus. Do not draw a thick, classically Gram-positive-style cell wall on either form.

GENUS-LEVEL cycle sequence: an EB attaches to a susceptible host epithelial cell and is taken up by an endocytosis-like process -> inside a membrane-bound vacuole (the INCLUSION), the EB differentiates into an RB over roughly the first 8-20 hours -> RBs replicate by binary fission, filling and expanding the inclusion (the inclusion can grow large enough to push the host cell's own nucleus aside, a genuinely observable and checkable feature in micrographs and cytology) -> from about 20-48 hours RBs begin asynchronously re-condensing back into EBs -> the host cell lyses (or, in some species/contexts, extrudes the inclusion) at roughly 48-72 hours, releasing infectious EBs to start the cycle in neighbouring cells. Sources differ slightly on exact hour ranges; NCBI Bookshelf gives an overall 36-50 h cycle, ABCD/veterinary sources describe C. felis specifically as taking about 48-72 h.

GENUS-LEVEL: on light-microscopy cytology (Giemsa/Romanowsky-stained conjunctival scrapes, the everyday diagnostic view, distinct from the ultrastructural EB/RB sizes above), the WHOLE INCLUSION appears as a basophilic (purple) cytoplasmic clump roughly 3-30 µm across depending on how far the cycle has progressed, typically pushed up against or capping the nucleus -- this is a useful visual composition cue but is a different scale than the individual 0.2-1 µm EB/RB particles resolved only by electron microscopy.

SPECIES-SPECIFIC (C. felis): near-exclusive tropism for conjunctival epithelium in cats, though it can also be recovered from the upper respiratory and, less commonly, GI/reproductive mucosa; the clinical picture is dominated by conjunctivitis with serous-to-mucopurulent, gummy ocular discharge, conjunctival hyperaemia and chemosis, most often in kittens/young cats (2 months to 1 year).

SPECIES-SPECIFIC (C. felis): transmitted by direct, close contact between cats via ocular and nasal secretions -- it survives poorly outside a host, so fomite transmission is possible but secondary; this is why prevalence concentrates wherever cats live in groups (shelters, catteries, multi-cat households), exactly as the catalogue text states.

SPECIES-SPECIFIC (C. felis): first-line treatment is a systemic antibiotic (doxycycline, ~10 mg/kg PO q24h for at least 4 weeks, per Merck Veterinary Manual) -- this is why the RB, not the EB, is the antibiotic-vulnerable target (EBs are metabolically near-dormant and comparatively antibiotic-insensitive; RBs are metabolically active and the ones antibiotics actually act on). A vaccine exists and reduces disease severity/shedding but does not fully prevent infection.

SPECIES-SPECIFIC (C. felis): zoonotic transmission to humans is possible but rare and generally mild -- documented cases are follicular conjunctivitis, mostly in people in close contact with an infected cat and sometimes immunocompromised (PMC case series, 2024). This is NOT an STI in cats or in the rare human cases -- that distinguishes it clearly from C. trachomatis in humans, which is sexually transmitted and a leading cause of infectious blindness (trachoma) in a different transmission context. Do not let the STI framing of C. trachomatis bleed into the C. felis text.
do_not_draw: A free-living, free-swimming bacterium dividing OUTSIDE a host cell in open medium -- chlamydiae cannot do this at any life stage; every RB shown dividing must be inside the inclusion, inside a host cell.
Flagella, cilia, or any whip-like/hair-like appendage on the EB or RB -- chlamydiae are completely nonmotile.

A virus capsid or icosahedral/phage-like geometric shell -- this is a bacterium (with its own DNA, ribosomes and a cell envelope), not a virus; do not give the EB an icosahedral or geometric faceted look.

A thick, classically Gram-positive-style peptidoglycan cell wall (a heavy uniform ring/shell) on either form -- the real envelope is thin and unusual (no substantial peptidoglycan layer); render it as a distinct but comparatively thin, taut outer boundary, especially on the EB.

The RB drawn smaller or denser than the EB, or the same size as the EB -- this is the single most important checkable error: EB must read as the SMALLER, DARKER/DENSER body; RB must read as the LARGER, PALER/more open-textured body. Getting this backwards defeats the entire teaching point.

EBs or RBs floating loose in the host-cell cytoplasm OUTSIDE the inclusion membrane -- both forms live and develop strictly inside the membrane-bound inclusion once the cycle has begun (an EB is only ever extracellular before it attaches/enters).

A cat, a person, or an eye anywhere in the four science-style renders (sem, textbook, 3d, watercolor) -- the subject is the cellular/ultrastructural cycle, not the whole animal or a clinical photo of a sick eye; keep those for the coloring page only, per the brief.

Blood, gore, pus, or a distressed/sick-looking animal -- this is a teaching subject for a children's atlas; the coloring page especially should be warm and reassuring (a cat with a flannel and a friendly eye-drop character), never showing the infection itself.

The human STI framing (genital tropism, sexual transmission) anywhere in the C. felis text -- that belongs to C. trachomatis in humans and must not be implied for the cat pathogen or the rare human zoonotic cases (which are ocular/conjunctival, from close animal contact, not sexual).

sources.note: NCBI Bookshelf, Medical Microbiology (Baron, ed.), chapter 'Chlamydia' -- genus-level EB size 0.25-0.3 um, RB size 0.5-0.6 um, nonmotile/no flagella, Gram-negative-like envelope, 36-50h developmental cycle stages (eclipse phase ~20h, growth, release), inclusion does not damage/displace... host nucleus remains a distinct visible organelle

Merck Veterinary Manual -- 'Chlamydial Conjunctivitis in Animals': C. felis forms inclusions in conjunctival epithelial cytoplasm, transmitted by direct close contact (fomite transmission secondary since chlamydiae survive poorly outside a host), young cats (2-6 months) most susceptible, doxycycline 10 mg/kg PO q24h for >=4 weeks first-line, vaccine gives incomplete protection, human zoonosis rare (one documented immunocompromised case of follicular conjunctivitis cited)

ABCD (European Advisory Board on Cat Diseases) -- 'GUIDELINE for Chlamydia felis': EB is extracellular/infectious/metabolically inactive and taken up by epithelial cells (phagocytosis-like uptake), differentiates into RB which multiplies inside a membrane-enclosed vacuole (the inclusion) avoiding lysosomal fusion, RBs redifferentiate to EBs released on host-cell lysis, full replication cycle ~2 days; EB antibiotic-insensitive vs RB antibiotic-sensitive; spreads via eye/nose secretions especially in group-housed cats (shelters/catteries)

PLOS ONE 2014 (Kokes/Valdivia lab or similar; GFP-Chlamydia developmental-cycle flow cytometry paper) -- EB ~0.3 um, rigid cell wall, densely packed DNA, reduced metabolic activity; RB 1-2 um, metabolically active, multiplies within the membrane-bound inclusion; RBs convert back to EB form before host-cell exit

eClinpath (Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine), October 2016 Case of the Month -- cytology-scale description of chlamydial inclusions on stained conjunctival scrapes (basophilic clumps, various substages/sizes on Giemsa/Romanowsky stain, typically capping the nucleus); a different (light-microscopy, whole-inclusion) scale than the ultrastructural EB/RB particle sizes above -- used here only for the 'inclusion caps/pushes the nucleus' composition cue, not for EB/RB dimensions

PMC (2024) -- 'Zoonotic transmission of Chlamydia felis from domestic cats: A case series of chronic follicular conjunctivitis in humans' -- documents that human infection is possible but rare and typically mild/ocular (follicular conjunctivitis), from close contact with an infected cat, not sexual transmission

PLOS Pathogens 2024 (Hovhannisyan et al.) -- 'Infection of human organoids supports an intestinal niche for Chlamydia trachomatis'; used as the source of the real-microscopy reference image (Fig. 6A) and its figure-legend colour code (blue arrowhead = EB, yellow arrowhead = RB) and stated 2 um scale bar; this paper studies C. trachomatis, not C. felis -- cited for the reference image and its genus-level developmental-form morphology only, not for any C. felis-specific claim

reference_search_log: Searched Wikimedia Commons (Category:Chlamydia trachomatis and MediaSearch), CDC Public Health Image Library (PHIL, advanced search for 'Chlamydia' -- results were clinical/light-microscopy photos, not clean single-inclusion TEM), and the (now-deleted from Flickr, only a small 500x250px mirror survives on Commons, CC BY 2.0) NIAID 'Correlative Light and Electron Micrograph of Infected HeLa Cells' composite -- rejected as reference because it is a 5-panel composite at only 500x250px total (each panel roughly 160x125px), far too small and cluttered with multiple panels/scale bars to isolate a clean single-inclusion crop. No freely-licensed Chlamydia felis-specific micrograph (TEM, SEM or otherwise) was found anywhere searched. Selected instead: PLOS Pathogens 2024 Fig. 6A (HeLa-cell panel), CC BY 4.0, native single-panel crop 535x516px from the published 1236x2220px figure PNG -- see chlamydia-felis.render.md SS2 for the full disclosure that this shows C. trachomatis, not C. felis.
